docs.title: Physics for Circuits: EE 2015
docs.text:
Circuits for Signal Processing — University of Minnesota

Welcome to the intelligent interactive textbook for EE 2015. This course covers the physics and mathematics of analog electrical systems with an emphasis on audio circuits and signal processing.

Textbook: James Nilsson & Susan Riedel, Electric Circuits, 11th Ed.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • Apply Kirchhoff's Voltage and Current Laws to analyze complex circuits
  • Use phasors and complex impedance to solve AC steady-state problems
  • Design and analyze first- and second-order filters (RC, RL, RLC)
  • Understand and use operational amplifiers in signal conditioning circuits
  • Decompose periodic signals using Fourier Series
  • Connect circuit theory to real audio and signal processing applications

docs.title: Course Structure
docs.text:
This textbook is organized into 16 chapters progressing from foundational physics through advanced signal processing:

Unit Topics Foundations (Ch. 1–5) Charge, voltage, current, power, Ohm's Law, Kirchhoff's Laws, circuit analysis Energy Storage (Ch. 6–8) Capacitors, inductors, transient and second-order circuits AC Analysis (Ch. 9–11) Sinusoids, phasors, complex impedance, AC power Signal Processing (Ch. 12–16) Op-amps, Bode plots, filters, Fourier Series, audio applications

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Each chapter includes:

  • Concept explanations with equations rendered in MathJax
  • MicroSims — interactive JavaScript simulations to visualize circuit behavior
  • Exercises to reinforce understanding
  • Glossary links for key terms

Start with the Course Description or jump directly to Chapter 1.

docs.title: EE 2015: Circuits for Signal Processing
docs.text: Institution: University of Minnesota Author: Prof. Sharat Batra Textbook: Nilsson & Riedel, Electric Circuits, 11th Ed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: EE 2015 introduces the analysis of analog electrical circuits with a focus on signal processing and audio applications. Students learn to model, analyze, and design circuits using fundamental laws and mathematical tools including phasors, Fourier Series, and Laplace transforms.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text:
Undergraduate electrical engineering students who have completed:

  • Calculus II (integrals, differential equations)
  • Physics II (electrostatics, basic circuits)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Differential and integral calculus
  • Basic physics: charge, electric field, Coulomb's law
  • Complex numbers (or willingness to learn)

docs.title: Topics Covered
docs.text:
1. Electric charge, current, voltage, and power
  2. Resistive circuits and Ohm's Law
  3. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) and Current Law (KCL)
  4. Node voltage and mesh current methods
  5. Thévenin and Norton equivalent circuits
  6. Capacitors and inductors as energy storage elements
  7. First-order RC and RL transient circuits
  8. Second-order RLC circuits and natural/step responses
  9. Sinusoidal steady-state analysis
  10. Phasors and complex impedance
  11. AC power: real, reactive, and apparent power
  12. Operational amplifiers: inverting, non-inverting, summing, differentiator, integrator
  13. Frequency response and Bode plots
  14. Low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, and notch filters
  15. Fourier Series representation of periodic signals
  16. Audio circuits and real-world signal processing applications

docs.title: Learning Outcomes (Bloom's Taxonomy)
docs.text:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Level Outcome Remember Recall fundamental laws: KVL, KCL, Ohm's Law, Faraday's Law Understand Explain the physical meaning of impedance, resonance, and bandwidth Apply Solve DC and AC circuit problems using node/mesh analysis Analyze Decompose a complex circuit into Thévenin/Norton equivalents Evaluate Choose appropriate filter topology for a given signal processing need Create Design a complete audio circuit (amplifier + filter) meeting given specifications

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Key terms for EE 2015: Circuits for Signal Processing.

Full glossary will be generated from the concept list.

docs.title: A
docs.text:
Admittance — The reciprocal of impedance; \(Y = 1/Z\), measured in siemens (S).

Amplitude — The peak value of a sinusoidal signal.

docs.title: B
docs.text:
Bandwidth — The range of frequencies over which a circuit's response is within 3 dB of its maximum value.

Bode Plot — A graph of a transfer function's magnitude (in dB) and phase versus frequency on a logarithmic scale.

docs.title: C
docs.text:
Capacitance — The ability of a component to store charge; measured in farads (F).

Cutoff Frequency — The frequency at which a filter's output power drops to half (−3 dB) of its passband value.

docs.title: F
docs.text: Fourier Series — A representation of a periodic signal as a sum of sinusoids at harmonically related frequencies.

docs.title: I
docs.text: Impedance — The complex ratio of phasor voltage to phasor current; \(Z = V/I\), measured in ohms (Ω).

docs.title: K
docs.text:
KCL (Kirchhoff's Current Law) — The algebraic sum of currents entering a node equals zero.

KVL (Kirchhoff's Voltage Law) — The algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop equals zero.

docs.title: O
docs.text: Op-Amp (Operational Amplifier) — A high-gain differential amplifier used as a building block in analog signal processing.

docs.title: P
docs.text:
Phasor — A complex number representing the amplitude and phase of a sinusoidal signal in steady state.

Power Factor — The cosine of the phase angle between voltage and current; \(\text{pf} = \cos\theta\).

docs.title: R
docs.text: Resonance — The condition in an RLC circuit where the impedance is purely real and the natural frequency equals the driving frequency.

docs.title: T
docs.text:
Thévenin Equivalent — A simplified model of a linear circuit consisting of a voltage source \(V_{Th}\) in series with a resistance \(R_{Th}\).

Time Constant (\(\tau\)) — The characteristic time for a first-order circuit to decay to \(1/e\) of its initial value.

Transfer Function — The ratio of output phasor to input phasor as a function of frequency; \(H(j\omega) = V_o/V_i\).

docs.title: Chapter 1: Electric Charge and Basic Quantities
Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the fundamental quantities of circuit analysis: electric charge, current, voltage, power, and energy. We establish the SI units used throughout the course and examine how circuit elements are modeled.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Electric charge and the coulomb
  2. Electric current: definition and units
  3. Voltage (electric potential difference)
  4. Power and energy
  5. SI units and prefixes
  6. Ideal circuit elements: sources and resistors
  7. Passive sign convention

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Basic physics: atoms, electrons, protons
  • Algebra and introductory calculus

docs.title: 1. Electric Charge
docs.text: Electric charge \(q\) is a fundamental property of matter, measured in coulombs (C). Electrons carry a charge of \(-1.602 \times 10^{-19}\) C.

docs.title: 2. Electric Current
docs.text:
Current \(i\) is the rate of flow of charge past a point:

\[i = \frac{dq}{dt}\]

The unit of current is the ampere (A), where \(1 \text{ A} = 1 \text{ C/s}\).

docs.title: 3. Voltage
docs.text:
Voltage \(v\) is the energy per unit charge required to move a charge between two points:

\[v = \frac{dw}{dq}\]

The unit of voltage is the volt (V), where \(1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J/C}\).

docs.title: 4. Power and Energy
docs.text:
Power \(p\) is the rate of energy transfer:

\[p = \frac{dw}{dt} = vi\]

Energy delivered over a time interval:

\[w = \int_{t_0}^{t} p \, d\tau = \int_{t_0}^{t} v \, i \, d\tau\]

docs.title: 5. Passive Sign Convention
docs.text:
Power is absorbed by an element when current enters the positive terminal:

\[p = +vi \quad \text{(absorbed)}\]

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. A current of 5 A flows through a wire for 3 seconds. How many coulombs pass through?
  2. If 60 J of energy is required to move 4 C of charge between two points, what is the voltage?
  3. A 12 V source delivers 2 A. What power does it supply?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter deepens the understanding of voltage, current, and power by introducing the passive sign convention, dependent sources, and power balance in circuits.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Passive sign convention (detailed)
  2. Independent voltage and current sources
  3. Dependent (controlled) sources
  4. Power absorbed vs. delivered
  5. Conservation of energy in circuits

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 1: Electric Charge and Basic Quantities

docs.title: 1. Passive Sign Convention
docs.text:
When current \(i\) enters the + terminal of an element with voltage \(v\):

\[p = vi \quad \text{(power absorbed)}\]

If \(p > 0\), the element absorbs power. If \(p < 0\), it delivers power.

docs.title: 2. Independent Sources
docs.text:
• Voltage source: maintains a specified voltage regardless of current
  • Current source: maintains a specified current regardless of voltage

docs.title: 3. Dependent Sources
docs.text:
Dependent sources have values controlled by a voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit. Four types:

Type Symbol Output VCVS \(\mu v_x\) Voltage controlled by voltage CCVS \(r i_x\) Voltage controlled by current VCCS \(g v_x\) Current controlled by voltage CCCS \(\beta i_x\) Current controlled by current

docs.title: 4. Power Balance
docs.text:
In any circuit, the sum of power delivered equals the sum of power absorbed:

\[\sum p_{\text{delivered}} = \sum p_{\text{absorbed}}\]

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. A dependent source \(2v_x\) is connected in a circuit where \(v_x = 3\) V. What voltage does it supply?
  2. Verify power balance in a simple circuit with one source and two resistors.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Resistive Circuits and Ohm's Law
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers Ohm's Law and the analysis of purely resistive circuits, including series and parallel combinations and voltage/current dividers.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Ohm's Law
  2. Resistance and conductance
  3. Series resistors and voltage divider
  4. Parallel resistors and current divider
  5. Power in resistive circuits
  6. Short and open circuits

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 2: Voltage, Current, and Power

docs.title: 1. Ohm's Law
docs.text:
\[v = iR\]

Resistance \(R\) is measured in ohms (Ω). Conductance \(G = 1/R\) is measured in siemens (S).

docs.title: 2. Series Resistors
docs.text:
\[R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_n\]

Voltage divider:

\[v_k = v_s \cdot \frac{R_k}{R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_n}\]

docs.title: 3. Parallel Resistors
docs.text:
\[\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{R_n}\]

For two resistors: \(R_{eq} = \dfrac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\)

Current divider:

\[i_k = i_s \cdot \frac{G_k}{G_1 + G_2 + \cdots + G_n}\]

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Three resistors (10 Ω, 20 Ω, 30 Ω) are in series across 60 V. Find the voltage across each.
  2. The same resistors are connected in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance and current through each.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law and Current Law are the two fundamental constraints governing all circuit analysis. This chapter develops both laws from first principles and applies them to multi-loop circuits.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Node, branch, and loop definitions
  2. Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
  3. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
  4. Applying KVL and KCL to solve circuits
  5. Planar vs. non-planar circuits

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 3: Resistive Circuits and Ohm's Law

docs.title: 1. Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
docs.text:
The algebraic sum of all currents leaving a node equals zero:

\[\sum_{k} i_k = 0\]

This is a consequence of conservation of charge.

docs.title: 2. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
docs.text:
The algebraic sum of all voltages around any closed loop equals zero:

\[\sum_{k} v_k = 0\]

This is a consequence of conservation of energy.

docs.title: 3. Applying KVL and KCL
docs.text: Steps: 1. Label all branch currents and node voltages 2. Apply KCL at each node (except reference/ground) 3. Apply KVL around each independent loop 4. Solve the resulting system of equations

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Use KCL and KVL to find all branch currents in a two-loop circuit.
  2. A ladder network has 4 nodes. Write the KCL equations.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces systematic methods for analyzing circuits: node voltage method, mesh current method, superposition, and Thévenin/Norton equivalents.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Node voltage method
  2. Mesh current method
  3. Superposition principle
  4. Thévenin equivalent circuit
  5. Norton equivalent circuit
  6. Maximum power transfer

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 4: Kirchhoff's Laws

docs.title: 1. Node Voltage Method
docs.text: Choose a reference node (ground). Assign voltages \(v_1, v_2, \ldots\) to all other nodes. Apply KCL at each non-reference node.

docs.title: 2. Mesh Current Method
docs.text: Assign mesh currents \(i_1, i_2, \ldots\) to each independent loop. Apply KVL around each mesh.

docs.title: 3. Superposition
docs.text: For linear circuits with multiple independent sources, the response equals the sum of responses due to each source acting alone (all others zeroed out).

docs.title: 4. Thévenin Equivalent
docs.text:
Any linear two-terminal circuit can be replaced by:

\[v = v_{Th} - i \cdot R_{Th}\]
  • \(v_{Th}\): open-circuit voltage
  • \(R_{Th}\): Thévenin resistance (with independent sources zeroed)

docs.title: 5. Norton Equivalent
docs.text: \[i = i_N - v / R_N \quad \text{where } R_N = R_{Th}, \quad i_N = v_{Th}/R_{Th}\]

docs.title: 6. Maximum Power Transfer
docs.text:
Maximum power is delivered to a load \(R_L\) when:

\[R_L = R_{Th}\] \[p_{max} = \frac{v_{Th}^2}{4 R_{Th}}\]

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Find the Thévenin equivalent seen by the load in a given circuit.
  2. Use superposition to find the output voltage with two independent sources.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Capacitors and inductors store energy in electric and magnetic fields, respectively. This chapter develops their voltage-current relationships and explains their behavior in DC and AC circuits.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Capacitor: structure and v-i relationship
  2. Energy stored in a capacitor
  3. Inductor: structure and v-i relationship
  4. Energy stored in an inductor
  5. Series and parallel combinations
  6. Continuity conditions

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 5: Circuit Analysis Techniques

docs.title: 1. Capacitor
docs.text:
\[i = C \frac{dv}{dt} \qquad v(t) = \frac{1}{C}\int_{-\infty}^{t} i \, d\tau\]

Energy stored:

\[w = \frac{1}{2} C v^2\]

Key property: Voltage across a capacitor cannot change instantaneously.

docs.title: 2. Inductor
docs.text:
\[v = L \frac{di}{dt} \qquad i(t) = \frac{1}{L}\int_{-\infty}^{t} v \, d\tau\]

Energy stored:

\[w = \frac{1}{2} L i^2\]

Key property: Current through an inductor cannot change instantaneously.

docs.title: 3. Series and Parallel
docs.text: Config Capacitors Inductors Series \(\frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \sum \frac{1}{C_k}\) \(L_{eq} = \sum L_k\) Parallel \(C_{eq} = \sum C_k\) \(\frac{1}{L_{eq}} = \sum \frac{1}{L_k}\)

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. A 10 μF capacitor is charged to 5 V. How much energy is stored?
  2. Find the equivalent capacitance of three 12 μF capacitors in series.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: First-order circuits contain one energy storage element. This chapter analyzes the natural and step responses of RC and RL circuits, introducing the concept of time constant.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Natural response of RC circuit
  2. Natural response of RL circuit
  3. Step response of RC circuit
  4. Step response of RL circuit
  5. Time constant \(\tau\)
  6. General first-order solution

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 6: Capacitors and Inductors

docs.title: 1. General First-Order Solution
docs.text:
For any first-order circuit, the response has the form:

\[x(t) = x(\infty) + [x(0^+) - x(\infty)] \, e^{-t/\tau}\]

where \(x(0^+)\) is the initial value, \(x(\infty)\) is the final value, and \(\tau\) is the time constant.

docs.title: 2. RC Circuit
docs.text:
\[\tau = RC\]
  • Natural response (source-free): \(v(t) = V_0 \, e^{-t/RC}\)
  • Step response: \(v(t) = V_s + (V_0 - V_s) e^{-t/RC}\)

docs.title: 3. RL Circuit
docs.text:
\[\tau = L/R\]
  • Natural response: \(i(t) = I_0 \, e^{-(R/L)t}\)
  • Step response: \(i(t) = \frac{V_s}{R} + \left(I_0 - \frac{V_s}{R}\right) e^{-(R/L)t}\)

docs.title: 4. Physical Interpretation
docs.text: After \(5\tau\), the circuit has reached ~99.3% of its final value — effectively steady state.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. An RC circuit has \(R = 10\) kΩ, \(C = 1\) μF, \(V_0 = 8\) V. Find \(v(t)\) and the time to reach 2 V.
  2. An RL circuit has \(R = 100\) Ω, \(L = 50\) mH. Find \(\tau\) and sketch \(i(t)\) for a 5 A initial current.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Second-order circuits contain two energy storage elements. This chapter analyzes the natural and step responses of series and parallel RLC circuits, introducing damping and resonance.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Characteristic equation of RLC circuits
  2. Natural frequency \(\omega_0\) and damping ratio \(\alpha\)
  3. Overdamped, critically damped, and underdamped responses
  4. Series RLC natural and step response
  5. Parallel RLC natural and step response
  6. Resonance frequency

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 7: First-Order Transient Circuits

docs.title: 1. Series RLC Circuit
docs.text:
The governing equation:

\[L \frac{d^2i}{dt^2} + R\frac{di}{dt} + \frac{i}{C} = \frac{dv_s}{dt}\]

Characteristic equation:

\[s^2 + \frac{R}{L}s + \frac{1}{LC} = 0\]

Parameters: - \(\alpha = R/(2L)\) — neper frequency (damping) - \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\) — resonant frequency - \(\omega_d = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \alpha^2}\) — damped natural frequency

docs.title: 2. Response Types
docs.text:
Condition Response \(\alpha > \omega_0\) Overdamped: two real roots \(\alpha = \omega_0\) Critically damped: repeated real root \(\alpha < \omega_0\) Underdamped: complex conjugate roots

Underdamped: \(x(t) = e^{-\alpha t}(A_1 \cos\omega_d t + A_2 \sin\omega_d t)\)

docs.title: 3. Parallel RLC Circuit
docs.text:
\[C \frac{d^2v}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{R}\frac{dv}{dt} + \frac{v}{L} = \frac{di_s}{dt}\]

Here \(\alpha = 1/(2RC)\).

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. A series RLC circuit has \(R = 8\) Ω, \(L = 1\) H, \(C = 1/16\) F. Determine the response type and find \(v(t)\) given \(v(0) = 4\) V, \(dv/dt(0) = 0\).
  2. Find \(\omega_0\) and \(\omega_d\) for the underdamped case above.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: When a circuit is driven by a sinusoidal source and transients have decayed, the circuit operates in sinusoidal steady state. This chapter introduces sinusoidal signals and the framework for steady-state AC analysis.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Sinusoidal signals: amplitude, frequency, phase
  2. Angular frequency \(\omega\) and period \(T\)
  3. Phase shift and lead/lag relationships
  4. RMS (root-mean-square) values
  5. Response of R, L, C to sinusoidal excitation

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 8: Second-Order RLC Circuits

docs.title: 1. Sinusoidal Signals
docs.text:
\[v(t) = V_m \cos(\omega t + \phi)\]
  • \(V_m\) — amplitude (peak value)
  • \(\omega = 2\pi f\) — angular frequency (rad/s)
  • \(\phi\) — phase angle (degrees or radians)
  • \(T = 1/f = 2\pi/\omega\) — period

docs.title: 2. RMS Values
docs.text:
For a sinusoid, the RMS value is:

\[V_{rms} = \frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}}\]

RMS values are used in power calculations: \(p_{avg} = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\theta\)

docs.title: 3. Response of Circuit Elements
docs.text: Element Relationship Resistor \(v = Ri\) — in phase Inductor \(v = L\,di/dt\) — voltage leads current by 90° Capacitor \(i = C\,dv/dt\) — current leads voltage by 90°

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. A sinusoidal voltage \(v = 10\cos(1000t + 30°)\) V. Find \(V_m\), \(f\), \(T\), \(\phi\), and \(V_{rms}\).
  2. Is \(v_1 = 5\cos(100t + 20°)\) leading or lagging \(v_2 = 5\cos(100t - 30°)\)?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Phasors transform sinusoidal steady-state analysis into algebra on complex numbers. This chapter develops the phasor representation and introduces complex impedance.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Phasor representation of sinusoids
  2. Phasor arithmetic
  3. Impedance of R, L, and C
  4. Admittance
  5. KVL and KCL in phasor domain
  6. AC circuit analysis using node/mesh methods

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 9: Sinusoidal Steady-State Analysis

docs.title: 1. Phasor Definition
docs.text:
A sinusoid \(v(t) = V_m\cos(\omega t + \phi)\) is represented as:

\[\mathbf{V} = V_m \angle \phi = V_m e^{j\phi}\]

The actual signal is recovered as: \(v(t) = \text{Re}[\mathbf{V} e^{j\omega t}]\)

docs.title: 2. Impedance
docs.text:
In the phasor domain, the v-i relationship becomes \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{Z}\,\mathbf{I}\):

Element Impedance \(\mathbf{Z}\) Resistor \(R\) Inductor \(j\omega L\) Capacitor \(\dfrac{1}{j\omega C} = \dfrac{-j}{\omega C}\)

docs.title: 3. Admittance
docs.text: \(\mathbf{Y} = 1/\mathbf{Z}\) — useful for parallel circuits.

docs.title: 4. AC Analysis Steps
docs.text:
1. Transform sources and elements to phasor domain
  2. Apply KVL/KCL, node voltage, or mesh current methods
  3. Solve for phasor voltages/currents
  4. Transform back to time domain

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Find the phasor current in a series RLC circuit driven by \(v_s = 10\cos(2000t)\) V with \(R = 5\) Ω, \(L = 1\) mH, \(C = 50\) μF.
  2. Convert the phasor result back to a time-domain sinusoid.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter analyzes power in AC circuits, distinguishing between real (average), reactive, and apparent power. Power factor and power factor correction are also introduced.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Instantaneous power
  2. Average (real) power \(P\)
  3. Reactive power \(Q\)
  4. Apparent power \(S\) and complex power
  5. Power factor and power factor angle
  6. Power factor correction
  7. Maximum average power transfer

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 10: Phasors and Complex Impedance

docs.title: 2. Average Power
docs.text:
\[P = \frac{1}{2} V_m I_m \cos(\theta_v - \theta_i) = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\theta\]

\(\theta = \theta_v - \theta_i\) is the power factor angle.

docs.title: 3. Complex Power
docs.text:
\[\mathbf{S} = P + jQ = \mathbf{V}_{rms}\,\mathbf{I}^*_{rms}\]
  • \(P\) = real power (watts, W) — energy consumed
  • \(Q\) = reactive power (volt-amperes reactive, VAR) — energy stored/returned
  • \(|\mathbf{S}|\) = apparent power (volt-amperes, VA)

docs.title: 4. Power Factor
docs.text:
\[\text{pf} = \cos\theta = \frac{P}{|\mathbf{S}|}\]

Lagging pf: inductive load (\(\theta > 0\)). Leading pf: capacitive load (\(\theta < 0\)).

docs.title: 5. Power Factor Correction
docs.text:
Add a capacitor in parallel to reduce \(|Q|\) and bring pf closer to 1:

\[C = \frac{Q_C}{\omega V_{rms}^2}\]

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. A load absorbs 1 kW at 0.8 lagging pf from a 120 V rms source. Find \(P\), \(Q\), \(S\), and \(I_{rms}\).
  2. What capacitance corrects the pf to unity at 60 Hz?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The operational amplifier (op-amp) is a versatile analog building block. This chapter introduces the ideal op-amp model and analyzes common configurations: inverting, non-inverting, summing, difference, integrator, and differentiator amplifiers.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Ideal op-amp model
  2. Negative feedback and virtual short
  3. Inverting amplifier
  4. Non-inverting amplifier
  5. Voltage follower (buffer)
  6. Summing amplifier
  7. Difference amplifier
  8. Integrator and differentiator

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 11: AC Power Analysis

docs.title: 1. Ideal Op-Amp Rules
docs.text:
When negative feedback is present:

  1. \(v_+ = v_-\) (virtual short — the two inputs are at equal voltage)
  2. \(i_+ = i_- = 0\) (no current flows into the input terminals)

docs.title: 2. Inverting Amplifier
docs.text: \[\frac{v_o}{v_i} = -\frac{R_f}{R_1}\]

docs.title: 3. Non-Inverting Amplifier
docs.text: \[\frac{v_o}{v_i} = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1}\]

docs.title: 4. Voltage Follower
docs.text: \[v_o = v_i \quad \text{(unity gain, high input impedance)}\]

docs.title: 5. Summing Amplifier
docs.text: \[v_o = -R_f\left(\frac{v_1}{R_1} + \frac{v_2}{R_2} + \cdots\right)\]

docs.title: 6. Integrator
docs.text: \[v_o(t) = -\frac{1}{RC}\int_0^t v_i \, d\tau\]

docs.title: 7. Differentiator
docs.text: \[v_o(t) = -RC\frac{dv_i}{dt}\]

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Design an inverting amplifier with gain \(-20\) using a 10 kΩ input resistor.
  2. A summing amplifier combines two signals: \(v_1 = 1\) V and \(v_2 = 2\) V through equal 10 kΩ resistors, with \(R_f = 20\) kΩ. Find \(v_o\).

docs.title: Chapter 13: Frequency Response and Bode Plots
Summary
docs.text: Frequency response describes how a circuit's output amplitude and phase vary with frequency. Bode plots are a standard tool for visualizing these characteristics on a logarithmic scale.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Transfer function \(H(j\omega)\)
  2. Magnitude and phase response
  3. Decibels (dB)
  4. Bode magnitude plot: poles and zeros
  5. Bode phase plot
  6. Bandwidth and cutoff frequency
  7. Resonance and quality factor \(Q\)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 12: Operational Amplifiers

docs.title: 1. Transfer Function
docs.text:
\[H(j\omega) = \frac{V_o(j\omega)}{V_i(j\omega)}\]

Magnitude: \(|H(j\omega)|\), Phase: \(\angle H(j\omega)\)

docs.title: 3. Bode Plot Rules
docs.text: Factor Magnitude slope Phase Zero at \(j\omega_z\) +20 dB/decade above \(\omega_z\) +45°/decade Pole at \(j\omega_p\) −20 dB/decade above \(\omega_p\) −45°/decade Gain \(K\) \(20\log_{10}K\) constant 0

docs.title: 4. Bandwidth
docs.text:
For a bandpass response, the bandwidth:

\[BW = \omega_{c2} - \omega_{c1}\]

Quality factor:

\[Q = \frac{\omega_0}{BW}\]

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Sketch the Bode magnitude plot for \(H(j\omega) = \frac{10}{1 + j\omega/100}\).
  2. A series RLC has \(R = 10\) Ω, \(L = 10\) mH, \(C = 10\) nF. Find \(\omega_0\), \(Q\), and \(BW\).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Filters selectively pass or attenuate signals based on frequency. This chapter covers the four fundamental filter types and their implementation using passive RLC elements and active op-amp circuits.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Low-pass filter (LPF)
  2. High-pass filter (HPF)
  3. Band-pass filter (BPF)
  4. Band-stop (notch) filter
  5. Passive RC and RLC filter design
  6. Active filters with op-amps
  7. Filter order and rolloff rate

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 13: Frequency Response and Bode Plots

docs.title: 1. Low-Pass Filter
docs.text:
Passes frequencies below \(\omega_c\), attenuates above.

RC LPF:

\[H(j\omega) = \frac{1}{1 + j\omega RC}, \qquad \omega_c = \frac{1}{RC}\]

docs.title: 2. High-Pass Filter
docs.text:
RC HPF:

\[H(j\omega) = \frac{j\omega RC}{1 + j\omega RC}, \qquad \omega_c = \frac{1}{RC}\]

docs.title: 3. Band-Pass Filter
docs.text:
Series RLC BPF:

\[H(j\omega) = \frac{j\omega R/L}{(j\omega)^2 + j\omega(R/L) + 1/(LC)}\]

Center frequency: \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\)

docs.title: 4. Band-Stop (Notch) Filter
docs.text: \[H(j\omega) = \frac{(j\omega)^2 + \omega_0^2}{(j\omega)^2 + j\omega(R/L) + \omega_0^2}\]

docs.title: 5. Active Filters
docs.text:
Op-amp filters can provide: - Gain without loading - Higher-order rolloff with cascading - Tunable cutoff frequency

Sallen-Key 2nd-order LPF is a common topology.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Design a passive RC low-pass filter with \(f_c = 1\) kHz.
  2. A band-pass filter needs center frequency 5 kHz and \(Q = 10\). Find \(BW\) and choose \(L\), \(C\), \(R\).

docs.title: Chapter 15: Fourier Series and Signal Decomposition
Summary
docs.text: Any periodic signal can be decomposed into a sum of sinusoids using Fourier Series. This chapter develops the Fourier Series representation and applies it to circuit analysis.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Periodic signals and harmonics
  2. Trigonometric Fourier Series
  3. Fourier coefficients \(a_n\), \(b_n\)
  4. Exponential Fourier Series
  5. Parseval's theorem and power spectrum
  6. Circuit response to periodic non-sinusoidal inputs
  7. Even and odd symmetry

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 14: Filters

docs.title: 1. Fourier Series Representation
docs.text:
A periodic signal \(f(t)\) with period \(T\) can be written as:

\[f(t) = a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[a_n \cos(n\omega_0 t) + b_n \sin(n\omega_0 t)\right]\]

where \(\omega_0 = 2\pi/T\) is the fundamental frequency.

docs.title: 2. Fourier Coefficients
docs.text: \[a_0 = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T f(t)\,dt\] \[a_n = \frac{2}{T}\int_0^T f(t)\cos(n\omega_0 t)\,dt\] \[b_n = \frac{2}{T}\int_0^T f(t)\sin(n\omega_0 t)\,dt\]

docs.title: 3. Exponential Form
docs.text: \[f(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n \, e^{jn\omega_0 t}\] \[c_n = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T f(t)\,e^{-jn\omega_0 t}\,dt\]

docs.title: 4. Symmetry Shortcuts
docs.text: Symmetry Non-zero terms Even (\(f(-t) = f(t)\)) \(a_n\) only (\(b_n = 0\)) Odd (\(f(-t) = -f(t)\)) \(b_n\) only (\(a_n = 0\)) Half-wave Odd harmonics only

docs.title: 5. Circuit Response
docs.text: Apply superposition: find the steady-state phasor response for each harmonic separately, then sum.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Find the Fourier Series of a square wave with amplitude \(A\) and period \(T\).
  2. A periodic signal is applied to an RC low-pass filter. Find the first three harmonics at the output.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This capstone chapter connects circuit theory to real audio signal processing applications, including microphone preamplifiers, equalizers, and loudspeaker crossover networks.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Audio frequency range (20 Hz – 20 kHz)
  2. Microphone preamplifier design
  3. Tone control and equalizer circuits
  4. Loudspeaker crossover networks
  5. Signal-to-noise ratio
  6. Total harmonic distortion (THD)
  7. End-to-end audio signal chain

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 15: Fourier Series and Signal Decomposition

docs.title: 1. Audio Frequency Range
docs.text: Human hearing spans approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Audio circuits must pass this band with minimal distortion.

docs.title: 2. Microphone Preamplifier
docs.text:
A microphone produces a low-level signal (~1 mV). A preamp uses a non-inverting op-amp stage:

\[A_v = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1}\]

Typical gain: 40–60 dB.

docs.title: 3. Tone Control Circuit
docs.text: A passive Baxandall tone control uses RC networks to boost/cut bass and treble independently.

docs.title: 4. Loudspeaker Crossover
docs.text:
A crossover splits the audio signal into frequency bands:

  • Woofer: low-pass (\(f_c \approx 300\) Hz)
  • Midrange: band-pass
  • Tweeter: high-pass (\(f_c \approx 3\) kHz)

Second-order Butterworth crossovers are common for 12 dB/octave rolloff.

docs.title: 5. Complete Signal Chain
docs.text:
\[\text{Microphone} \to \text{Preamp} \to \text{Equalizer} \to \text{Power Amp} \to \text{Crossover} \to \text{Speakers}\]

At each stage, apply the circuit analysis techniques from this course.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Design a non-inverting preamp with 40 dB gain and input impedance > 10 kΩ.
  2. Design a second-order passive crossover with crossover frequency 2.5 kHz for an 8 Ω load.
  3. Sketch the full Bode plot of the complete signal chain you designed.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
Q: What math do I need before starting this course? You need calculus through integration and basic differential equations, complex numbers, and introductory physics (charge, electric fields). A comfort level with algebra and trigonometry is assumed throughout.

Q: What textbook does this course use? Electric Circuits, 11th Ed., by James Nilsson and Susan Riedel.

docs.title: Circuit Analysis
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between KVL and KCL? KVL (Kirchhoff's Voltage Law) applies to loops and says voltage drops sum to zero. KCL (Kirchhoff's Current Law) applies to nodes and says currents sum to zero. Both must be satisfied simultaneously in any circuit.

Q: When should I use node voltage vs. mesh current method? Use node voltage when there are fewer independent nodes than meshes, or when the circuit has current sources. Use mesh current when there are fewer independent loops than nodes, or when the circuit has voltage sources.

Q: What does a Thévenin equivalent tell me? It replaces any linear circuit with a simple voltage source + series resistor. This is especially useful for analyzing what happens when you connect different loads.

docs.title: AC and Phasors
docs.text:
Q: Why do we use phasors? Phasors convert differential equations into algebraic equations by working in the frequency domain. This makes AC circuit analysis as straightforward as DC analysis.

Q: What does "lagging power factor" mean? A lagging power factor means the current waveform lags the voltage waveform in phase — characteristic of inductive loads. It means reactive power is being stored and returned to the source, reducing efficiency.

docs.title: Filters and Op-Amps
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a passive and active filter? A passive filter uses only R, L, C components with no gain. An active filter includes an op-amp, which can provide gain and prevent loading between stages.

Q: How do I choose between a low-pass and high-pass filter? Decide which frequencies you want to keep. Low-pass keeps low frequencies (bass sounds, slow signals). High-pass keeps high frequencies (treble, fast transients).
